L	Article 14 of the Indian Constitution states that the State shall not deny to any person equality
before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India. It can be conferred
from this statement that no one is above the law of the land and the Rule of Law shall prevail as all
are equal in the eyes of law. But this rule is not absolute and is subject to many exceptions.
The Rule of Law cannot prevent a certain class of persons from being subject to special laws, hence,
the State has the power to make laws operating differently on different classes of people, in a way
that the principle of equality of civil rights and equal protection of law is followed. This is being
known as the 'Doctrine of Reasonable Classification’.
Article 14 permits Reasonable Classification and not Class Legislation. Class Legislation means
making of improper discrimination by conferring certain privileges upon a class of persons
arbitrarily selected from a huge number of people. Thus, Class legislation violates equal protection
whereas, Reasonable Classification is always based on real and substantial distinction.
Case Law:
In Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Justice S.R. Tendolkar, AIR 1958, the Supreme Court held that: It is
now well established that while Article 14 forbids class legislation, it does not forbid reasonable
classification for the purposes of legislation. It condemns discrimination not only by a substantive
law but also by a law of procedure.
Hence, Article 14 forbids the class legislation but it does not forbid reasonable classification,
however, these classifications must not be ‘arbitrary, artificial or evasive’. In the case of State of
West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar, the Supreme Court of India, stated the twin test for reasonable
classification. The court held that for the classification to pass the test, two conditions must be
fulfilled:
i. Classification must be founded on an intelligible differentia which distinguishes those that are
grouped together from others and
ii. The differentia must have a rational relation to the object sought to be achieved by the Act.
Relevance:
The court said that:
The differentia which is the basis of the classification and the object of the act are distinct things
and what is necessary is that there must be a nexus between them i.e. the object of the law and the
grouping.
The doctrine of reasonable classification is mere judicial test to determine whether there is
arbitrariness in the state action if the state action in question does not pass the test as laid down
by the doctrine it is considered arbitrary and since it is arbitrary it will be unconstitutional as per
the principles of article 14. This ensures that people similarly situated are treated equally.

Classification.pdf

1.	A newly elected government, claiming to advance the constitutional ideal of equality, introduces
the Uniform Civic Benefits Act, 2026. Under the Act, every citizen, irrespective of age, disability,
economic background, educational attainment, or social disadvantage, is entitled to receive
identical public benefits and is subjected to identical legal obligations. Defending the legislation,
the government argues that any differentiation among citizens is inherently inconsistent with
equality because Article 14 requires the State to treat all persons exactly alike.
Assuming the government's understanding of equality is accepted, which of the following
propositions would most likely be rejected by contemporary Indian constitutional jurisprudence?
(a) Equality permits differential treatment where distinctions are founded on relevant differences
and bear a legitimate connection with the objective sought to be achieved.
(b) Identical treatment of all persons is the highest manifestation of constitutional equality,
irrespective of differences in circumstances.
(c) Treating unequals alike may, in certain situations, produce substantive inequality rather than
equality.
(d) Constitutional equality is concerned not merely with uniformity of treatment but also with
preventing arbitrary State action.

For several decades, challenges under Article 14 were predominantly examined through the lens of
reasonable classification, requiring courts to determine whether a law was founded upon an
intelligible differentia and whether such differentia bore a rational nexus to the object sought to be
achieved. Over time, constitutional courts recognised that certain State actions could satisfy the
formal requirements of classification and yet remain fundamentally incompatible with the
constitutional guarantee of equality.
Which of the following doctrines emerged most significantly to address this limitation in Article 14
jurisprudence?
(a) Doctrine of Eclipse, which permits revival of pre-constitutional laws upon the removal of
constitutional inconsistencies.
(b) Doctrine of Territorial Nexus, which enables legislatures to enact laws having extra-territorial
operation when a sufficient connection exists.
(c) Doctrine against Arbitrariness, which recognises that arbitrary State action may violate
equality even in the absence of an impermissible classification.
(d) Doctrine of Pith and Substance, which determines the true nature and character of legislation
in cases involving legislative competence.
I.	Until 2023, India did not have a standalone law or framework to govern data protection. The
Information Technology Act, 2000 (IT Act) and rules notified thereunder formed the basis around
which the data protection framework revolved. This included the Information Technology
(Reasonable Security Practices and Procedures and Sensitive Personal Data or Information) Rules,
2011 (Privacy Rules).
In 2017, a constitutional bench of nine judges of the Supreme Court of India in Justice K. S.
Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India upheld that privacy is a fundamental right, which is
entrenched in Article 21 [Right to Life & Liberty] of the Constitution of India. This led to the
process of formulation of a comprehensive data protection framework for India. After releasing
different draft versions of a data protection legislation and considering the recommendations from
different stakeholders, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY),
Government of India, released the draft of the Digital Personal Data Protection Bill in 2022 (DPDP
Bill).
The version of the DPDP Bill which was eventually passed by both houses of the Indian Parliament
marked a few significant changes to the original draft of the DPDP Bill. On August 11, 2023, the
Government of India published that version as the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023
(DPDP Act), which would form the personal data protection and regulatory regime in India. The
DPDP Act introduces several compliances with respect to the collection, processing, storage and
transfer of digital personal data. However, further actions on behalf of the Government are
required to make the DPDP Act effective, including notifying the sections of the DPDP Act itself,
repealing the Privacy Rules and notifying the rules and regulations required for effective
implementation and enforcement of the DPDP Act. www.lawpreptutorial.com
The DPDP Act is applicable only to personal data in digital form and does not regulate non-
personal and non-digital data. Considering this, collection and handling of non-personal data is
currently unregulated in India.

IV.	Dowry-related fatalities reliably trigger choreographed cycles of legislative indignation,
prosecutorial posturing, and performative collective mourning — yet the socioeconomic
substructure that inexorably generates such violence emerges from each episode of public outrage
structurally uncontested, institutionally reinforced, and culturally resanctified. This recursive
contradiction constitutes perhaps the most consequential and deliberately unacknowledged market
failure embedded within India's social economy: a polity that statutorily criminalises dowry while
systematically legitimising its operational logic through euphemistic reclassification — financial
extractions repackaged as familial gifting, status capitalisation, or economically rational
compensation accruing to the male-headed provisioning household. Matrimony in India functions
less as a voluntary interpersonal arrangement than as a sophisticated multi-dimensional
institution — concurrently executing caste boundary enforcement, intergenerational capital
transfer, gendered labour allocation, and hierarchical social mobility negotiation. Within this
institutional architecture, transactional expectations are not peripheral aberrations but
structurally determined outputs of the system's own internal logic. Violence, therefore, resists
analytical disaggregation from the institution itself; it represents the most visible downstream
manifestation of legitimised economic asymmetry, operationalised within household units where
women disproportionately absorb unremunerated care labour, sacrifice professional capital, and
bear asymmetric responsibility for relational preservation — a systematically feminised
productivity cost that neither markets price nor policymakers adequately account for. The
institution's more insidious coercive mechanisms operate beneath the threshold of juridical
visibility entirely: the manufactured social panic surrounding unmarried women of advancing age,
the structural delegitimisation of alternative domesticity arrangements, and the categorical
expectation that intimacy, economic security, and social belonging must be accessed exclusively
through sanctioned matrimonial channels. What presents phenomenologically as autonomous
individual choice routinely operates within profoundly constrained decision environments where
viable structural alternatives have been methodically denied institutional recognition, resource
allocation, and cultural legitimacy. Legislative intervention, however procedurally indispensable,
addresses symptomatic manifestations while leaving foundational determinants operationally
undisturbed. Substantive reform demands something considerably more architecturally disruptive
— the deliberate redistribution of care infrastructure, the institutional scaffolding of collective
living arrangements, and the political willingness to systematically decouple human dignity,
belonging, and security from their near-total dependence upon the privatised matrimonial
household as civilisation's singular legitimate organising unit.

XIV. The Doctrine of Colourable Legislation is an important principle of constitutional law that prevents
legislatures from indirectly doing what they are not permitted to do directly. It is often described as
a “fraud on the Constitution” because it checks attempts by legislative bodies to exceed their
constitutional authority while appearing to act within legal limits. The doctrine originates from the
Latin maxim “quando aliquid prohibetur ex directo, prohibetur et per obliquum,” which means that
what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly. In India, this doctrine was adopted from
Canadian and Australian constitutional practices during British rule and later became an integral
part of constitutional jurisprudence after independence. The doctrine primarily examines the
legislative competence of Parliament and State Legislatures.
It comes into operation when a legislature enacts a law on a subject over which it has no authority,
but disguises the legislation in a manner that makes it appear valid. The courts then look beyond
the form of the law to determine its real substance and purpose. If the true nature of the legislation
reveals that the legislature has trespassed into a field outside its constitutional powers, the law
may be declared void. This doctrine is closely linked to Article 246 of the Constitution of India,
which distributes legislative powers between the Union and the States through the Union List,
State List, and Concurrent List. By applying this doctrine, courts ensure that neither Parliament
nor State Legislatures encroach upon each other’s constitutionally assigned domains.
However, the doctrine has certain limitations. It applies only to questions of legislative competence
and not to the wisdom, necessity, or motives behind a law. It is also generally inapplicable where
there are no constitutional restrictions on legislative power and does not usually extend to
subordinate legislation. The intention of the legislature, whether good or bad, is not the focus; the
only concern is whether the law falls within its constitutional authority. A significant case related
to this doctrine is R.S. Joshi v. Ajit Mills (1977), where the Supreme Court clarified that colourable
legislation arises when a legislature lacks the power to enact a law but attempts to create the
appearance of possessing such authority. Thus, the doctrine serves as an essential safeguard for
maintaining constitutional balance and federal governance in India.

XIX. Contracts of indemnity and contracts of guarantee are special types of contracts under the Indian
Contract Act, 1872 that deal with the allocation of risk and liability. A contract of indemnity,
defined under Section 124 of the Act, is a contract by which one party promises to save another
from loss caused to him by the conduct of the promisor himself or by the conduct of any other
person. In such a contract, there are two parties: the indemnifier (who promises to compensate)
and the indemnified (who is protected from loss). The primary purpose of an indemnity contract is
to provide security against potential loss, and liability arises only when there is actual loss suffered
by the indemnified party. A common example is an insurance contract, where the insurer
indemnifies the insured against specified losses.
On the other hand, a contract of guarantee is defined under Section 126 of the Indian Contract Act
as a contract to perform the promise or discharge the liability of a third person in case of his
default. It involves three parties: the surety (who gives the guarantee), the principal debtor (who
owes the obligation), and the creditor (to whom the guarantee is given). The objective of a
guarantee is to provide assurance to the creditor that the debt or obligation will be fulfilled. Unlike
indemnity, the liability of the surety is secondary and arises only when the principal debtor
defaults. A guarantee may be either oral or written, although in practice it is usually documented.
A surety’s liability is co-extensive and not dependent on prior suit against debtor.
The key difference between indemnity and guarantee lies in the nature of liability and the number
of parties involved. In indemnity, liability is primary and independent, whereas in a guarantee,
liability is secondary and conditional upon default by the principal debtor. Furthermore, indemnity
involves only two parties, while guarantee involves three. Another important distinction is that
indemnity focuses on compensation for loss, whereas guarantee focuses on ensuring performance or
payment of another person’s obligation.
These concepts are widely used in commercial transactions, banking, insurance, and financial
agreements to reduce risk and ensure trust between parties. The Supreme Court of India has also
clarified in various judgments that the distinction between indemnity and guarantee must be
determined based on the substance of the contract rather than its form or title. Thus, both these
contracts play a crucial role in facilitating secured commercial dealings in modern legal systems.
